fields.expected: Something that doesn't show up on a resume: my cofounders and I got a meeting with Hopkins President Ron Daniels by knocking on a locked door. It was during Lighting of the Quads, we realized he was nearby, walked to Garland Hall, saw him through the glass, and knocked until someone let us pitch. That thirty-second conversation turned into a formal meeting months later with him and leadership from the Data Science and AI Institute. I bring it up because it corrected something I believed. I used to think the hard part of a project was the build, and everything else was overhead. With ClarityAtlas I wrote the iOS app, the passive sleep estimation from HealthKit and Core Motion signals, and the backend matching service, and none of that mattered until we recruited users into the pilot and convinced people at the institution it should exist. The other thing not on my resume is how much time I spend reading about how research gets funded and evaluated, and cold-emailing researchers and science-policy people to ask why they think the system works the way it does. Several of those conversations changed my mind.

fields.expected: I work most with PyTorch, XGBoost, and scikit-learn on the modeling side, and with LLM tooling (OpenAI APIs, embeddings, retrieval-augmented generation, Pinecone vector search, and a Neo4j graph for relational memory) on the applied side. At Summer Atlantic Capital I built the ML core of an anomaly-detection system, including temporal sequence modeling over event streams with RNN/Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, a learning-to-rank layer for alert prioritization, and an RAG explanation layer served through a versioned FastAPI microservice. For interpretability and causal work I have used SHAP-based feature selection and G-formula simulations on a ~10M-record survey dataset. I am also comfortable with LLM evaluation as its own engineering problem: at Intelehealth I designed a stratified-sampling evaluation framework comparing model-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard, and in tSearch I built a rubric-driven multi-judge LLM assessment pipeline where missing evidence is reported as insufficient evidence rather than a low score. On the agent side I use Playwright with TypeScript/Node and Zod validation, with LLM calls confined to narrow, gated call sites.
